text.brief: Wei Jingsheng landed in Detroit on November 16, 1997 after nearly eighteen years in the Party's prisons.
text.record: The Party released him on medical parole two weeks after Jiang Zemin's state visit to Washington and sent him abroad rather than home. In April 1998 it sent the student leader Wang Dan to the United States two months before Bill Clinton's visit to the mainland ([State Department 1998 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: China](https://1997-2001.state.gov/global/human_rights/1998_hrp_report/china.html); [Human Rights Watch chronology: China, Hong Kong, Tibet (April-June 1998)](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/campaigns/china-98/chron298.htm)). Neither man could return. After Clinton left, courts sentenced the founders of the China Democracy Party to long prison terms ([State Department 1998 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: China](https://1997-2001.state.gov/global/human_rights/1998_hrp_report/china.html); [Human Rights Watch: Nipped in the Bud, the suppression of the China Democracy Party (2000)](https://www.hrw.org/report/2000/09/01/china-nipped-bud/suppression-china-democracy-party)).
text.reading: The Party traded prisoners for summits and kept the power to take more, so each release bought a visit while the prisons stayed full. Exile removed the critic from the country and turned a moral cost into a diplomatic credit, which is Stratagem 17.
text.gapText: Architecture Principles. Washington counted releases as progress and set no price for the arrests that replaced them.
text.fix: Count arrests and releases on one ledger, and judge a summit on the net.
